challenges.name: classify-sync-failures-quiz
challenges.title: Retry later, or give up now?
challenges.description: A sync client that retries everything blocks the queue forever; one that gives up too easily throws away a technician's work. Sort the failures.

questions.question: The field-service app flushes its outbox and send() fails. Which of these failures should keep the mutation in the outbox so a later flush sends it again? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A 503 and a network TypeError say nothing about the mutation itself - the same request can succeed later, so the edit must stay queued. A TypeError from fetch carries no status code at all; treating unknown errors as transient protects the user's data, and the worst case is one more attempt. A 422 (invalid data) and a 403 (no longer allowed to edit the job) will fail identically on every retry: keeping them would block every later edit of that record. Report them, park them where the user or support can see them, and move on.

options.text: The API gateway answers 503 Service Unavailable during a deploy.
fetch() rejects with TypeError: Failed to fetch because the van is in a tunnel.
The server answers 422 because the technician entered a negative part quantity.
The server answers 403 because the dispatcher reassigned the job to another technician.

challenges.name: outbox-sync-client
challenges.title: Build the outbox sync client
challenges.description: Implement createSyncClient({ send, maxInFlight }) with enqueue(mutation) and flush(). Coalesce unsent edits of the same record, never touch an entry that was already sent, send one mutation per record at a time and at most maxInFlight records at once, keep transient failures (and everything queued behind them) for the next flush, report permanent ones, and resolve flush() with a summary of what was sent, what failed and what is still pending.

tests.name: Unsent edits of the same record are merged into one mutation
At most maxInFlight records sync at once; a second flush() call joins the first
An edit made while its record is syncing waits for that call to finish
Retryable failures stay queued unchanged; permanent ones are reported
An unknown network error keeps the record's edits; other records still sync

challenges.name: idempotent-mutation-id-quiz
challenges.title: The edit that vanished on retry
challenges.description: Mutation ids let the server ignore duplicates. Combine that with a well-meant optimisation and see what happens.

questions.question: The server stores every processed mutation id and, when it sees an id again, returns the stored result without applying anything. The client sends m-41 { status: 'done' } for job-42. The server applies it, but the response is lost in a tunnel, so the client keeps m-41 in the outbox. The technician then captures the customer's signature, and the client merges { signature: 'sig-9' } into m-41 because 'it was never confirmed anyway'. On the next flush m-41 is sent again. What is the result?
questions.explanation: To the server, m-41 is a duplicate: it was processed once, so the stored result is returned and the new payload is never applied. The client removes m-41 as 'sent' and the signature is lost silently. (A stricter server may reject the reused id because the payload changed - the edit still does not land.) Once a mutation has been sent, its id and content are frozen: new edits must go into a new mutation with a new id, queued behind it. That is also why PATCH being 'usually safe to retry' is not a guarantee - HTTP does not define PATCH as idempotent; the mutation id is what makes retries safe.

options.text: The server applies the signature, because the payload is different from the first request.
The status is applied a second time and the job's history shows two 'done' events.
The signature is never stored: the server treats m-41 as an already-processed duplicate, and the client then drops m-41 as successfully sent.
Nothing goes wrong: PATCH requests are idempotent by definition, so the server merges both versions.
